rows.original: גֹּאֵל הַדָּם הוּא יָמִית אֶת הָרֹצֵחַ (35:19); וְרָצַח גֹּאֵל הַדָּם אֶת הָרֹצֵחַ אֵין לוֹ דָּם (35:27)
rows.translation: KJV ('revenger of blood'), JPS 1917 ('avenger of blood') and Douay-Rheims ('kinsman' in 35:19, 'avenger of blood' in 35:27), read directly; Masoretic Hebrew
rows.says: 'The revenger of blood himself shall slay the murderer: when he meeteth him' (35:19, 21), where the killing was in hatred, lying in wait or enmity. One who killed without enmity is judged by the congregation, delivered from the avenger and restored to his city of refuge until the high priest dies (35:22 to 25). If he goes beyond its border 'and the revenger of blood find him ... and ... kill the slayer; he shall not be guilty of blood' (35:27; JPS 'there shall be no bloodguiltiness for him'; Douay-Rheims 'he shall not be guilty that killed him'), because he should have stayed until the high priest's death (35:28).
rows.bearing: The strongest counted text against K1 and K0. In 35:27 a kinsman, whom rule 5 names as a private actor, kills on his own initiative, with no court ordering it, a person the congregation had found to be an unintentional killer and who threatens no one, and the text declares him wholly blameless because of what the victim did (leaving the refuge). On the plain words of rules 2 and 5 that is Contradicted, for all branches. It is Unclear rather than Contradicted on two grounds, both now read directly: (1) the counted texts set the avenger inside a scheme of judgement (35:12 'until he stand before the congregation in judgment'; 35:24 to 25; 35:29 'a statute of judgment'; Deuteronomy 19:12; Joshua 20:4 to 6; 2 Samuel 14:11), so whether he acts as the law's appointed executor (exclusion (a)) or privately is disputed (rule 5, last sentence); (2) the tradition's own counted texts forbid private vengeance and give the 'revenger' role to the ruler (Romans 12:19; 13:4), a narrowing by counted texts (rule 6). Both grounds are contestable: no court orders the 35:27 killing, and that Romans 12:19 reaches Numbers 35 is the tradition's reading, made explicit only by Tier 2 authorities (Aquinas II-II q.64 a.3). No Christian classical comment on 35:27 itself was found. For K0, the Hebrew go'el means redeemer or next of kin (Douay-Rheims 'kinsman'), so 'revenger' is a translators' reading, and 35:27 states no motive: a disputed word (rule 6).

rows.says: Israel joins Baal Peor and God's anger burns. God tells Moses to hang the chiefs, and Moses tells 'the judges of Israel, Slay ye every one his men' who joined Baal Peor (25:5). If Phinehas acted as a private zealot, rules 2 and 5 make K1 Contradicted in every branch. Whether it was private is disputed within the counted texts: it follows Moses' order to the judges (25:5), Phinehas was of the priestly line, Psalm 106:30 reads 'executed judgment' (KJV) or 'wrought judgment' (JPS) but 'pacified' (Douay-Rheims) or 'made atonement' (Brenton), and 1 Maccabees 2:24 to 26 (Catholic and Orthodox) presents Phinehas-like zeal as acting 'according to judgment'. K0: the motive is zeal or jealousy (qin'ah) for God, not on its face one of K0's motives: Implied at most. K3: not war in this passage, though war with Midian follows.

K1.label: Unclear (all branches)
K1.reason: Taught at the Explicit level, for everyone, in counted texts every branch accepts, all now read directly: Exodus 20:13 and Deuteronomy 5:17; Genesis 9:5 to 6 (every human being, as made in God's image); Leviticus 24:17 and 24:22 (one law for stranger and native); Exodus 21:12 to 14 with Numbers 35:31 (no ransom for a murderer); Matthew 5:21 to 22 and 19:18; Romans 13:9 to 10 and James 2:11, with the reach of 'neighbour' set by Luke 10:29 to 37, Luke 6:27 to 35 and Matthew 5:43 to 48. Named groups: newborns and children (Exodus 1:15 to 21; Psalm 106:37 to 38; Leviticus 18:21 and 20:2 to 5; Jeremiah 7:31), slaves (Exodus 21:20), strangers (Jeremiah 22:3; 2 Samuel 12:9), the wicked (Genesis 4:15), religious outsiders (Luke 9:54 to 56), crowds and zealots (John 8:7; John 16:2; 1 Timothy 1:13), and private avengers (Romans 12:17 to 21; 1 Samuel 25:26 and 25:33; 2 Samuel 3:27 to 39 with 1 Kings 2:31 to 33). Against this, two counted texts accepted by every branch approve a deliberate killing of people who threaten no one, by actors rule 5 names as private. (1) Numbers 35:26 to 28 (read directly in KJV, JPS 1917, Douay-Rheims and Hebrew): a kinsman who finds a court-judged unintentional slayer outside his city of refuge and kills him 'shall not be guilty of blood'; no court orders the killing. (2) Numbers 25:7 to 13 with Psalm 106:30 to 31 (read directly): God rewards Phinehas for spearing Zimri and Cozbi, and it is 'counted unto him for righteousness'. On the plain words of rules 2 and 5 these would give Contradicted. They give Unclear because, for each, whether the act is judicial or private is disputed within the tradition's own counted texts (rule 5, last sentence; rule 6), all read directly. For the avenger: Numbers 35:12, 35:24 to 25 and 35:29 ('a statute of judgment'), Deuteronomy 19:12, Joshua 20:4 to 6 and 2 Samuel 14:11 place him inside a scheme of judgement under the congregation, elders and king; and Romans 12:19 with 13:4 forbids private vengeance and names the ruler God's 'revenger' (KJV) or 'avenger' (Douay-Rheims), the title the Torah gives the go'el. For Phinehas: Numbers 25:5 has Moses order the judges to slay the offenders; Psalm 106:30 reads 'executed judgment' (KJV) or 'wrought judgment' (JPS) against 'pacified' (Douay-Rheims) and 'made atonement' (Brenton, search); and 1 Maccabees 2:24 to 26 (Catholic and Orthodox) describes Phinehas-like zeal as acting 'according to judgment'. Further hard cases, each Unclear at most and none deciding alone: Exodus 21:21 (a slave who dies after a day or two; intent disputed); Exodus 22:2 to 3 (a burglar killed while breaking in; presumed danger disputed, and the daylight clause limits it); Deuteronomy 13:6 to 10 (relatives who entice to other gods; the 'hand first' clause matches the witnesses' role in 17:7, and Brenton has 'report', but the Douay-Rheims has 'presently put him to death'). Reports without approval are Implied and do not decide (rule 4): 1 Kings 18:40, Genesis 22, Judges 11, Genesis 38:24, Exodus 2:12 and Samson (Judges 14 to 16; divine empowerment, war context). The divine-command exception in Augustine and Aquinas is Tier 2 and decides nothing. How close the result is: both grounds for Unclear are contestable. No court orders the 35:27 killing, and that Romans 12:19 reaches a Mosaic licence is the tradition's reading (made explicit by Aquinas II-II q.64 a.3, Tier 2), not stated in the text; no Christian classical comment on 35:27 itself was found. If the lead holds, as the households annex did for New Testament limits on Exodus 21:20 to 21, that later counted texts limit but do not narrow an earlier permission, and that the avenger in 35:27 acts on his own authority, the label becomes Contradicted (all branches). It becomes Taught only if the avenger is read as the law's executor (exclusion (a)) and Phinehas as judicial. Consistency: Judaism's provisional Contradicted on the same verse rests on its counted Rabbinic reading (Mishnah Makkot 2:7), which confirms a private licence; Christianity's different result rests only on its own counted New Testament texts. The same structure appears in Abū Dāwūd 4361 (a killing declared free of retaliation because of what the victim did): if no counted narrowing is found there, the different label is justified only by the narrowing here, and the lead should confirm that this distinction is accepted. Branch notes: the deuterocanon (1 Maccabees 2, Judith 9, Wisdom 12) speaks for Catholics and Orthodox only and cannot carry a finding alone; Jubilees 30 (Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo only; VERIFIED (search)) approves the Shechem killing and could give 'Contradicted in one branch' (rule 3) if that church is a major branch under decision 3 and the attack is not read as war; corpus.md does not yet decide this.

K0.label: Unclear (all branches)
K0.reason: Each motive is taught Explicitly or as Clear teaching in counted texts every branch accepts, all read directly. Gain: Deuteronomy 27:25 ('taketh reward to slay an innocent person'), Proverbs 1:10 to 19 ('greedy of gain; which taketh away the life of the owners'), 1 Kings 21:19 and 2 Samuel 12:9. Anger: Matthew 5:21 to 22, Genesis 4:5 to 11 and Genesis 49:5 to 7 ('in their anger they slew a man ... Cursed be their anger'). Hatred: 1 John 3:15 and Leviticus 19:17 (fellow believers and kin), widened by Luke 6:27 to 35 and Matthew 5:43 to 48. Revenge: Romans 12:17 to 21, Matthew 5:38 to 39, 1 Samuel 25:26 and 25:33, and the condemnation of Joab's revenge killing of Abner (2 Samuel 3:27 to 39; 1 Kings 2:5 and 2:31 to 33); Leviticus 19:18 is taught in part. The deciding hard case is Numbers 35:26 to 28 (read directly): the killer licensed and declared guiltless is the go'el ha-dam, 'revenger' (KJV) or 'avenger' (JPS) of blood, whom Deuteronomy 19:6 expects to pursue 'while his heart is hot' (KJV, JPS; Hebrew כִּי יֵחַם לְבָבוֹ). But go'el means redeemer or next of kin (the Douay-Rheims has 'kinsman' in Numbers 35:19 and Deuteronomy 19:12, and 'pushed on by his grief' in 19:6), and 35:27 states no motive, so whether the licensed killing is 'out of revenge' is a disputed word (rule 6); and whether it is judicial or private, and narrowed by Romans 12:19 and 13:4, is disputed as for K1 (rules 5 and 6). So Unclear. Phinehas's motive is zeal or jealousy for God (Numbers 25:11), not on its face one of K0's motives. Samson's killings (Judges 14:19, gain and anger after the Spirit of the LORD comes; 15:7 and 16:28, revenge; Hebrews 11:32) are reported without a statement that they were right (rule 4: Implied) and are set in the conflict with Philistine rule (14:4; 15:11): war context or a hard case, not deciding. Psalm 137:9 blesses a revenge killing of infants, but in a lament about a city's destruction: war context, Implied. For Catholics and Orthodox only: 1 Maccabees 2:24 approves a killing done in 'anger according to judgment' (Unclear: judicial, ruler or war context disputed), and Judith 9:2 is a prayer ascribing to God the sword 'to take vengeance' at Shechem (Implied); neither can carry a finding alone. Jubilees 30 (Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo only; not in corpus.md) approves the Shechem revenge killing as righteousness and could give 'Contradicted in one branch' (rule 3) if that church is a major branch and the attack is not read as war. What would change the label: if the 35:27 killing is counted as revenge by a private actor and Romans 12:19 is not accepted as a narrowing, Contradicted (all branches); if the go'el is read as the law's executor, Taught (all branches).

K3.label: Contradicted (all branches)
K3.reason: Counted texts accepted by every branch, all now read directly, command or approve the deliberate killing in war of people who are not fighting. Deuteronomy 20:16 to 17: in the cities of the named nations 'thou shalt save alive nothing that breatheth ... as the Lord thy God hath commanded thee'. 1 Samuel 15:3: 'Thus saith the Lord of hosts' ... 'slay both man and woman, infant and suckling'; Saul is rejected for sparing the captive king Agag (15:9 to 23), whom Samuel then 'hewed ... in pieces before the Lord' (15:33). Numbers 31:17: Moses, angry that the captive women were spared, orders 'kill every male among the little ones'. Joshua 6:21 (with 6:2 and 6:27): Jericho's 'man and woman, young and old' are destroyed, and 'the Lord was with Joshua'. These meet rules 2 and 4 (God or the lawgiver commands or approves). For Catholics and Orthodox, Wisdom 12:3 to 6 adds that it was God's will to destroy the old inhabitants 'by the hands of our fathers'. Tier 1 teaches K3 in part (read directly): women and little ones of distant cities are spared, though every male is killed (Deuteronomy 20:13 to 14); Elisha forbids killing captives (2 Kings 6:21 to 23); ripping up pregnant women is condemned (Amos 1:13; 2 Kings 8:12); soldiers are told 'Do violence to no man' (Luke 3:14). Psalm 137:9 is a lament (Implied). The tradition explains the commands as unique divine commissions (Augustine, Contra Faustum XXII.74 to 75; Aquinas II-II q.64 a.6 ad 1; Tier 2, verified by search in project records only) and teaches non-combatant immunity today (Catechism 2313 to 2314; Vitoria; unverified). Later authorities never outweigh a contradicting counted text (decision 7). K3 is a record wording and does not affect the floor.

direct.direct_count: Of 77 rows, 64 are Tier 1 (all branches, or Catholic and Orthodox for the deuterocanon), and all 64 are now VERIFIED (direct) in the KJV, KJV Apocrypha or Douay-Rheims (scrollmapper, third-party copies) and, for Old Testament rows, also in Sefaria's JPS 1917 and Masoretic Hebrew. Of these, 57 bear on a label (support, limits, counter rows, hard cases and counted reconciliations) and 7 are context only (court, before birth, accident, acts of God); all are direct. Every deciding row is direct: for K1 and K0, Numbers 35:26 to 28 and its judicial frame (Numbers 35:12, 24 to 25, 29 to 30; Deuteronomy 19:1 to 13; Joshua 20; 2 Samuel 14:11), Numbers 25:1 to 18, Psalm 106:28 to 31, Exodus 21:21, Exodus 22:2 to 3, Deuteronomy 13:6 to 11 and 17:2 to 7, and the narrowing texts Romans 12:17 to 21 and 13:1 to 4, Luke 9:54 to 56 and Matthew 5:38 to 39; for K3, Deuteronomy 20:16 to 17, 1 Samuel 15:3 and 15:33, Numbers 31:17 and Joshua 6:21. Parts still only search-verified: Brenton's Septuagint readings of Psalm 105:30 ('made atonement') and Deuteronomy 13:9 ('report'), which bear on the Orthodox reading of two hard cases; and Jubilees 30 (outside corpus.md; Ethiopian Orthodox only), seen only in a search summary. Not read at all: the Greek of every New Testament row and of the Septuagint (no local copy), and WEBBE, the project's main translation. The 13 Tier 2 or outside-corpus rows (Augustine, Aquinas, Basil, the catechisms and confessions, Matthew Henry, the Didache and Fathers, Luther) are not available locally and decide nothing; they keep their earlier status (search-verified in project records, or UNVERIFIED), except Aquinas II-II q.64 a.3, where one search added the opening of the reply to objection 1. Six web searches were used; the budget was 10.

objections.label: K1
objections.objection: Numbers 35:26 to 28 is the exact case that rules 2 and 5 describe, and neither ground for Unclear holds. (a) Rule 2 names 'a text that declares such a killing wholly blameless ... because of ... what the victim did'. 35:27 to 28 does just that: 'he shall not be guilty of blood ... Because he should have remained in the city'. (b) Rule 5 names 'a kinsman' as a private actor, and the Douay-Rheims itself calls the go'el 'the kinsman' (35:12, 35:19, 35:21) and 'the next of kin' (35:24). (c) No court or ruler orders the killing. The only judgement in the passage protects the slayer: the congregation 'shall deliver the slayer out of the hand of the revenger' (35:25), and the elders 'shall not deliver the slayer up into his hand' (Joshua 20:5). (d) The counted texts say outright that there is no death sentence for this slayer. In Deuteronomy 19:6 he is 'not worthy of death' (KJV), 'not deserving of death' (JPS 1917) or 'not guilty of death' (Douay-Rheims). The Hebrew is ולו אין משפט מות, 'for him there is no judgment (mishpat) of death'. 19:10 calls his blood 'innocent blood', and the Douay-Rheims calls him 'the innocent' at Numbers 35:25. (That last point should not be pressed alone, because at 35:26 the same version calls him 'the murderer', translating the same Hebrew word.) So the 35:27 killing cannot be a court's death sentence being carried out. It is a statutory licence to a private kinsman. (e) The 'judicial scheme' texts (35:12, 35:24 to 25, Deuteronomy 19:12, Joshua 20:4 to 6) govern the hearing and the handing over of a convicted murderer. The research's own Deuteronomy 19 row concedes that they do not cover the 35:27 case. 2 Samuel 14:11 is rated Implied (a case staged by Joab). The phrase 'statute of judgment' in 35:29 (KJV, JPS) heads the whole law; the Douay-Rheims has only 'an ordinance'. (f) If a Torah statute were enough to make the person it licenses a court officer, rule 5 would cover no one, because every master, father and kinsman text in the Torah is a statute. The same applies to treating God as Israel's ruler, so that every Torah licence becomes 'a ruler's order'. (g) Rule 5's last sentence needs the judicial or private character to be 'disputed within the tradition'. The research found no Christian comment on 35:27 at all. A dispute the researchers build from the structure of the text is not a dispute within the tradition. The rows themselves say that 'on the plain words of rules 2 and 5 these would give Contradicted' and that both grounds for Unclear are 'contestable'.
objections.rule_basis: Rules 2 (last clause), 5 (named private actors; last sentence requires a dispute within the tradition) and 6; exclusion (a) covers punishment imposed through a court or ruler, which Deuteronomy 19:6 rules out here. Passages read directly for this objection: Numbers 35:9 to 34 (KJV, Douay-Rheims; JPS 1917 for 35:25, 35:27 and 35:29); Deuteronomy 19:1 to 13 (KJV, Douay-Rheims; JPS 1917 and Masoretic Hebrew for 19:6 and 19:10); Joshua 20:1 to 9 (KJV).
objections.proposed: Contradicted (all branches), decided by Numbers 35:26 to 28. It falls to Unclear only if a verified Christian classical or counted reading treats the 35:27 killing as carrying out the congregation's sentence, or if the project lead rules that a statutory licence following a court judgement falls under exclusion (a). Either change must then be applied to Judaism on the same verse.

objections.label: K1
objections.objection: Romans 12:17 to 21 with 13:1 to 4 limits Christian conduct but does not narrow Numbers 35:27, so it cannot ground Unclear under rule 6. (a) Romans 12:19 quotes Deuteronomy 32:35 ('To me belongeth vengeance'), and Leviticus 19:18 already said 'Thou shalt not avenge'. Both stood in the Torah beside Numbers 35:27 without cancelling it. Restating a principle that already sat beside the licence cannot, on its own, narrow the licence. (b) Neither verse mentions the avenger, the cities of refuge or the Mosaic law. The rows admit that applying them to 35:27 is 'the tradition's reading ... not stated in the text'. (c) The link through 'revenger' is an English echo. The KJV uses 'revenger' in Numbers 35 and in Romans 13:4. The Douay-Rheims has 'avenger' in Romans 13:4 but 'kinsman' in Numbers 35:19. The Greek was not read (none is available locally). The Septuagint's word for the go'el should be compared with the word in Romans 13:4 before anything rests on the echo; my memory is that they differ, but that is unchecked and I do not rely on it. (d) Precedent: the households annex kept Exodus 21:20 to 21 'Contradicted' for Christianity, although Ephesians 6:9 and Colossians 4:1, which speak directly to masters, teach the opposite. They were recorded as teaching beside the contradiction, not as narrowing it (annex, Christianity summary). Romans 12:19 is less on point than those texts. (e) Internal consistency: the Christianity K3 reason rightly holds that the tradition's account of the commanded destruction as unique and superseded does not remove the contradiction (decision 7). By the same logic, the end of the judicial law (Romans 13:4 as read by the tradition; Aquinas I-II q.104 a.3; Westminster 19.4) limits when the licence applies, not what it permitted. (f) The Tier 2 readings do not narrow it either. Aquinas II-II q.64 a.3 is general. Its reply to objection 1 (an act belongs to the one by whose authority it is done), like Augustine's City of God I.21 (killing allowed under God's 'general law'), would place the avenger's licence under divine law, which is the divine-command exception K1 lacks. Applied, they would confirm the licence, not deny it. Neither was found commenting on 35:27.
objections.rule_basis: Rule 6 (narrowing by counted texts or classical commentators); decision 7; the households annex treatment of New Testament household texts beside Exodus 21:20 to 21; the Christianity K3 reasoning. Read directly: Romans 12:17 to 21 and 13:1 to 4 (KJV), Romans 12:19 and 13:4 (Douay-Rheims), Deuteronomy 32:35, Leviticus 19:17 to 18 (KJV).
objections.proposed: Drop Romans 12:19 with 13:4 as a ground for Unclear. Record it as Explicit teaching of K0 and K1 for Christians, beside the contradiction. Before the echo argument is used again, check the Greek of Romans 13:4 against the Septuagint of Numbers 35.

objections.label: K1
objections.objection: Phinehas stays Unclear, but the reasoning cites 1 Maccabees 2 on the wrong side and leaves out the strongest judicial point. 1 Maccabees 2:24 says 'according to judgment' (KJV Apocrypha) or 'according to the judgment of the law' (Douay-Rheims). That means in line with the law's verdict, carried out on the spot by a man who held no hearing: the zealot model rule 5 names. Read with 2:26 ('like as Phinees did unto Zambri') and 2:54, it supports the private reading of Phinehas for Catholics and Orthodox. Only 2:17 weighs against this (the king's officers call Mattathias 'a ruler'). In those branches' Bibles, Psalm 105:30 has 'pacified' (Douay-Rheims) or 'made atonement' (Brenton), with no judicial verb. So for them the judicial reading of Phinehas rests on Numbers 25:5. That verse is strong. In the Douay-Rheims it reads 'Let every man kill his neighbours, that have been initiated to Beelphegor', a ruler's order (exclusion (a)) that reaches Zimri. Cozbi, a Midianite, falls outside that order but inside the hostility of 25:16 to 18 (war context). So Unclear stands for all branches, on Numbers 25:5 against 25:7 ('rose up from among the congregation') and the praise of his own zeal, not on 1 Maccabees 2.
objections.rule_basis: Rules 4, 5 and 6; exclusions (a) and (b). Read directly: Numbers 25:1 to 15 (KJV, Douay-Rheims), Psalm 106:28 to 31 (KJV) and 105:28 to 31 (Douay-Rheims), 1 Maccabees 2:15 to 28 and 2:49 to 58 (Douay-Rheims), 2:23 to 27 and 2:54 (KJV Apocrypha).
objections.proposed: Keep Phinehas as Unclear (all branches) and correct the reason: 1 Maccabees 2 leans to the private reading, and Numbers 25:5 carries the judicial one.

objections.label: K0
objections.objection: The 'disputed word' ground does not hold for Christianity, so K0 stands or falls with K1's judicial or private question. Every Bible read names the licensed killer at 35:25 to 27 as revenger or avenger: KJV 'revenger of blood' (35:27); JPS 1917 'avenger of blood' (35:27); Douay-Rheims 'revenger' (35:25) and 'avenger of blood' (35:27). The Douay-Rheims 'kinsman' appears at 35:12, 35:19, 35:21 and Deuteronomy 19:12, not at 35:27. The etymology of go'el (redeemer) is not how any branch's Bible renders this verse. Deuteronomy 19:6 shows that the law expects the avenger to pursue 'while his heart is hot' (KJV, JPS 1917; Hebrew כי יחם לבבו) or 'pushed on by his grief' (Douay-Rheims). It names that as the danger the refuge guards against, and 35:27 removes the guard outside the border. The licensed killing pays back a kinsman's death, on a man the same law says has no sentence of death (Deuteronomy 19:6). Nothing else in the text explains it: there is no danger, no sentence, and no cleansing of the land, since the high priest's death serves that (35:25 and 35:28). That '35:27 states no motive' does not help. Rule 2 asks whether the text permits a killing the wording forbids, and a permission with no condition on motive includes the case done in hot anger that Deuteronomy 19:6 expects. Unlike the Judaism record, Christianity has no counted reading (such as Rabbi Yose the Galilean's 'duty') that even arguably recasts the motive.
objections.rule_basis: Rules 2, 5 and 6 (a disputed word must be disputed in the tradition's own texts or readings). Read directly: Numbers 35:12 to 29 (KJV, Douay-Rheims; JPS 1917 for 35:25 and 35:27), Deuteronomy 19:6 (KJV, JPS 1917, Douay-Rheims, Masoretic Hebrew).
objections.proposed: Contradicted (all branches), resting on Numbers 35:26 to 28 with Deuteronomy 19:6. If the lead keeps K1 Unclear on the judicial or private question, K0 is Unclear on that ground (and on Phinehas: next objection), not on the meaning of go'el.

objections.label: K0
objections.objection: Phinehas is a hard case for K0, not 'Implied at most', so the reason's fallback 'if the go'el is read as the law's executor, Taught (all branches)' is wrong. In Numbers 25:11 his zeal is God's own: he 'turned my wrath away ... while he was zealous for my sake'. For Catholics and Orthodox, 1 Maccabees 2:24 to 26 describes Phinehas-like zeal as anger ('shew his anger', KJV Apocrypha) or wrath ('his wrath was kindled', Douay-Rheims), and approves it by the comparison. Whether K0's 'anger' reaches religious zeal is a question of reach (rule 6), as other traditions' records treat religious-penalty killings. So if 35:27 were resolved in Christianity's favour, K0 would still be Unclear: at least in the Catholic and Orthodox branches, and arguably in all, since Numbers 25:11 is in every Bible and its judicial or private character is itself disputed.
objections.rule_basis: Rules 3, 4, 5 and 6; the corpus.md deuterocanon rule bars only a whole-tradition finding that rests on the deuterocanon alone, not a branch-level one under rule 3. Read directly: Numbers 25:11 to 13 (KJV, Douay-Rheims); 1 Maccabees 2:24 to 26 (KJV Apocrypha, Douay-Rheims).
objections.proposed: Record Phinehas as Unclear for K0 (all branches; reinforced for Catholic and Orthodox by 1 Maccabees 2:24 to 26). Remove 'Taught (all branches)' as a possible outcome while it stands.

objections.label: K1
objections.objection: Luke 9:54 to 56 is used as 'the tradition's counter-reading to zealot precedents (Elijah in the KJV text)' and set against 1 Kings 18:40. 'Even as Elias did' refers to calling fire down from heaven on the king's soldiers (2 Kings 1:10 to 12), which is God's act, not to the slaughter at the Kishon by human hands. The rebuke is Clear teaching against wanting a village of religious outsiders destroyed. It is not a narrowing reading of 1 Kings 18:40, of Phinehas or of any avenger text.
objections.rule_basis: Rules 4 and 6. Read directly: Luke 9:54 to 56 and 2 Kings 1:9 to 12 (KJV).
objections.proposed: Keep Luke 9:51 to 56 as support (Clear teaching for K1's reach and K0). Remove the claim that it answers 1 Kings 18:40 or the zealot texts.

objections.label: K1
objections.objection: The reason lists 2 Samuel 3:27 to 39 with 1 Kings 2:31 to 33, and 1 Samuel 25, under 'private avengers' and as part of the reconciliation. Joab avenges a brother killed in battle ('the blood of war in peace', 1 Kings 2:5), and David's intended revenge on Nabal answers an insult. Neither is a go'el case under Numbers 35. They show that revenge outside the law is condemned (good support for K0). They do not show that the 35:27 licence is narrowed. The consistency remark also misdescribes Judaism. On rules 2 and 5 the Torah verse itself gives Contradicted, and the Mishnah only stops a fall to Unclear. As I read the Judaism record, its label is for all branches, Karaites included, who do not accept the Mishnah. Christianity stands on the same verse in the same position.
objections.proposed: Reword: these texts support K0 and K1 against revenge outside the law, and do not bear on the licence in Numbers 35:27. State that Judaism's label rests on the Torah verse, with the Mishnah confirming.

objections.label: K0
objections.objection: Samson comes closer to approval of a killing for gain than 'Implied' suggests. Judges 14:4 says it 'was of the Lord'. In 14:19 the Spirit of the Lord comes on him, he kills thirty men of Ashkelon and takes their garments to pay a wager, 'and his anger was kindled'. Hebrews 11:32 to 33 names him among those who 'wrought righteousness'. But 14:4 frames the whole matter as the struggle against Philistine 'dominion over Israel', and Samson judged Israel, so it is war context or at most a hard case (Unclear). Hebrews 11:33 praises the faith of a list of people, not this act.
objections.rule_basis: Rules 4, 5 and 6; exclusion (b). Read directly: Judges 14:4, 14:19 and Hebrews 11:32 to 34 (KJV).
objections.proposed: Rate Samson as a hard case (Unclear at most; war context), not as Implied. It does not decide K0.

objections.label: K3
objections.objection: Luke 3:14 ('Do violence to no man') is counted as teaching K3 in part. It is said to soldiers together with 'neither accuse any falsely; and be content with your wages': it is about extortion and abuse of people under their power, not killing in war. Also tested and rejected in the gentler direction: the tradition's reading of the commands as unique, time-bound divine commissions (Augustine, Contra Faustum XXII.74 to 75; Origen's allegory) limits when the commands applied, not whom they reached once they applied. So it does not narrow them under rule 6, and decision 7 keeps the counted texts decisive.
objections.rule_basis: Rules 2, 4, 6 and 7; decision 7. Read directly: Luke 3:14 (KJV).
objections.proposed: Rate Luke 3:14 as Implied for K3. The label stays Contradicted (all branches).

K1.label: Contradicted (all branches)
K1.reason: Support: Tier 1 teaches K1 at the Explicit level, for everyone, in texts every branch accepts. These include Exodus 20:13, Genesis 9:5 to 6, Leviticus 24:17 and 24:22, Exodus 21:12 to 14 with Numbers 35:31, Matthew 5:21 to 22, Romans 13:9 to 10 and James 2:11, with the reach set by Luke 10:29 to 37, Luke 6:27 to 35 and Matthew 5:43 to 48. Newborns and children are named (Exodus 1:15 to 21; Psalm 106:37 to 38). Against this, Numbers 35:26 to 28 (Tier 1, all branches, read directly in the KJV, Douay-Rheims, JPS 1917 and Hebrew) lets the dead man's kinsman, with no court or ruler ordering it, kill a man the congregation has judged an unintentional slayer, once he is found outside his city of refuge. It declares the kinsman free of bloodguilt because of what the victim did. That is rule 2's own example, and rule 5 names the kinsman as a private actor. The counted texts rule out the judicial reading. Deuteronomy 19:6 says this slayer has no sentence of death (Hebrew ולו אין משפט מות; KJV 'not worthy of death'), 19:10 calls his blood innocent, and the congregation's only ruling saves him from the avenger (Numbers 35:25; Joshua 20:5). No Christian reading putting the 35:27 killing inside a court's sentence was found, so the judicial or private character is not 'disputed within the tradition' (rule 5). Romans 12:19 with 13:4 forbids private vengeance to Christians. But the same principle already stood beside the licence in the Torah (Deuteronomy 32:35, which Romans quotes; Leviticus 19:18). The verses never mention the avenger. The link through 'revenger' is an English echo whose Greek was not checked. Under the households annex precedent and decision 7, a later teaching limits but does not narrow an earlier permission. The classical readings (Augustine, City of God I.21; Aquinas II-II q.64 a.3), if applied, would place the licence under God's law, a divine-command exception K1 does not have. Further hard cases, each Unclear and none deciding alone: Phinehas (Numbers 25:7 to 13 with Psalm 106:30 to 31; Moses' order in 25:5 against his own initiative and praised zeal); Exodus 21:21 (intent); Exodus 22:2 to 3 (presumed danger); Deuteronomy 13:6 to 10 (the witnesses' role, as Deuteronomy 17:7; the Douay-Rheims also keeps 'afterwards the hands of all the people'). The reports in 1 Kings 18:40, Genesis 22, Judges 11, Genesis 38:24 and Exodus 2:12 are Implied. How close: the label rests on how one verse is classed. The best case for Unclear is exclusion (a)'s 'as each tradition's law defines it', since the Torah makes the go'el the agent of blood redress (Deuteronomy 19:12). But Deuteronomy 19:6 shows that 35:27 carries out no sentence. What would change it: a verified Christian classical or counted reading that the 35:27 killing executes the congregation's sentence, or a ruling by the project lead that a statutory licence after a court judgement is exclusion (a). Either gives Unclear (on Phinehas), never Taught while Phinehas is disputed, and must be applied to Judaism alike.

K0.label: Contradicted (all branches)
K0.reason: Each motive is taught Explicitly or as Clear teaching in texts every branch accepts. Gain: Deuteronomy 27:25 and Proverbs 1:10 to 19. Anger: Matthew 5:21 to 22 and Genesis 49:5 to 7. Hatred: 1 John 3:15, widened by Luke 6:27 to 35. Revenge: Romans 12:17 to 21, Matthew 5:38 to 39, 1 Samuel 25:33, and 2 Samuel 3:27 to 39 with 1 Kings 2:31 to 33. Against this, Numbers 35:26 to 28 (Tier 1, all branches, read directly) licenses a private kinsman to kill, without guilt, a man the law says has no sentence of death. In every Bible read, the licensee is named at that point as the revenger or avenger of blood: KJV 35:27; JPS 1917 35:27; Douay-Rheims 35:25 'revenger' and 35:27 'avenger of blood'. Deuteronomy 19:6 says the law expects him to pursue 'while his heart is hot' (KJV, JPS 1917; Hebrew כי יחם לבבו) or 'pushed on by his grief' (Douay-Rheims). The licensed killing pays back the kinsman's death and serves no other purpose stated in the text. A licence with no motive condition, given to the avenger as avenger, permits the killing in anger and revenge that the law itself expects (rule 2). The Douay-Rheims 'kinsman' (35:12, 35:19, 35:21) and the etymology of go'el do not make the word disputed at 35:27, and Christianity has no counted reading that recasts the motive as a duty. This label depends on K1's classification of 35:27 as private. If the project lead keeps K1 Unclear on the judicial or private question, K0 is Unclear on that ground, not on the meaning of go'el. Phinehas is a further hard case (Unclear, all branches), not Implied. In Numbers 25:11 his zeal turns away God's 'wrath', and for Catholics and Orthodox 1 Maccabees 2:24 to 26 calls Phinehas-like zeal 'anger' or 'wrath' and approves it. So K0 could not be Taught even if 35:27 were read as judicial. Samson (Judges 14:4, 14:19; Hebrews 11:32) is a hard case set in war (exclusion (b)), Unclear at most. Psalm 137:9 is a war lament (Implied). Judith 9:2 is a prayer (Implied). Jubilees 30 is outside corpus.md and does not decide.

K3.label: Contradicted (all branches)
K3.reason: Texts every branch accepts, all read directly by the research, command or approve the deliberate killing in war of people who are not fighting, infants included. Deuteronomy 20:16 to 17: 'save alive nothing that breatheth', as God commanded. 1 Samuel 15:3: 'infant and suckling'; Saul is rejected for sparing the captive Agag, and Samuel kills him 'before the Lord' (15:33). Numbers 31:17: Moses orders the captive boys and women killed. Joshua 6:21 with 6:27. Even the ordinary rule of war has every male of a captured distant city killed (Deuteronomy 20:13). For Catholics and Orthodox, Wisdom 12:3 to 6 adds that God willed the destruction 'by the hands of our fathers'. Tier 1 teaches K3 in part: women and little ones of distant cities are spared (Deuteronomy 20:14); Elisha forbids killing captives (2 Kings 6:21 to 23); ripping up pregnant women is condemned (Amos 1:13; 2 Kings 8:12). Luke 3:14 concerns soldiers' extortion and is Implied only. Psalm 137:9 is a lament (Implied). The tradition reads the commands as unique divine commissions and teaches non-combatant immunity today (Augustine, Contra Faustum XXII.74 to 75; Aquinas II-II q.64 a.6 ad 1; Catechism 2313 to 2314, unverified). These readings limit when the commands applied, not whom they reached, so they do not narrow them (rule 6), and later authorities never outweigh a contradicting counted text (decision 7). K3 is a record wording and does not affect the floor.

challenge.consistency_notes: 1. Numbers 35:26 to 27 (Judaism and Christianity). The same verse under the same rules gives Contradicted for both. Rule 2's last clause and rule 5's named kinsman apply to the Torah text itself. Judaism's counted Mishnah (Makkot 2:7) confirms a private licence and so stops a fall to Unclear; it is not what makes the verse contradict. As I read the Judaism record, its label covers all branches, the Karaites included, who do not accept the Mishnah. A different label for Christianity therefore needs a real Christian narrowing, and none was found. Romans 12:19 restates Deuteronomy 32:35 and Leviticus 19:18, which stood beside the licence in the Torah. It never mentions the avenger. Treating it as a narrowing would also clash with the households annex, where Ephesians 6:9 and Colossians 4:1, addressed directly to masters, did not narrow Exodus 21:20 to 21 for Christianity. Labelling Christianity Unclear and Judaism Contradicted on the same verse would favour one tradition. 2. Phinehas (Numbers 25 with Psalm 106:30 to 31).
